sample_unit: human participants (compared with LLM persona-simulated responses)

links.outcome: Alignment of LLM persona-simulated patient responses with real human responses on discharge summaries
links.effect: LLM personas aligned better on information items than perception items, underselected 'I don't know' responses, and did not capture heterogeneous responses; authors conclude simulation should complement, not replace, human evaluation.
links.quote: Persona-based LLM simulation should be used as an assistive screening tool for patient materials and should complement, not replace, human evaluation with subgroup validation.

links.outcome: Subgroup differences in LLM simulation alignment with human responses by education and gender
links.effect: Every model aligned more closely with the high-education than the low-education subgroup on information items; gender differences were smaller and inconsistent; equity performance varied substantially across models.
links.quote: Education was the most consistent stratification axis: every model aligned more closely with the high-education subgroup than with the low-education subgroup on information items, suggesting that LLMs capture broad factual-comprehension differences associated with educational background.

Chain-of-thought prompting to improve simulated response alignment

screen.reason: Empirical study testing whether persona-prompted LLM simulation can reliably approximate patient comprehension of discharge summaries across demographic subgroups as a pre-deployment screening safeguard.

primary.practice: persona-based simulation testing of patient-facing materials
